title: A minimal mechanism to generate long timescales without fine tuning
authors: Kathryn McClain, Shivang Rawat, Mia Morrell, Stefano Martiniani, David J. Heeger, Flaviano Morone
abstract: Long timescales in brain dynamics give rise to power law correlations measured in experiments. A simple linear recurrent neural network model can reproduce this power law behavior, but the recurrent interaction strength needs to be fine tuned in order to sit at the edge of stability. We show that by adding a dynamical recurrent feedback gain to the simple linear model removes the need for fine tuning, because the gain self-organizes so that the spectrum of the effective recurrent matrix is always gapless with the top eigenvalue landing on the stability edge for any recurrent strength. As a consequence, long timescales and scale free correlations arise generically, as we demonstrate both analytically and numerically.
summary: This work proposes a minimal modification to a linear recurrent neural network by adding a dynamical feedback gain. This gain self-regulates the network's dynamics, ensuring that the system naturally operates at a critical point, thereby generating long-range, scale-free temporal correlations without requiring precise parameter tuning.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of generating long timescales and scale-free correlations in neural dynamics without relying on fine-tuning of synaptic coupling strengths.
main_result: Introducing a dynamical recurrent feedback gain self-organizes such that the top eigenvalue of the effective recurrent matrix always lands at the stability edge, leading to scale-free correlations generically.
method: The analysis involves linearizing the coupled dynamics (neuron activity and gain) around an active fixed point and analyzing the resulting relaxation rates and correlation functions.
model_or_system: The system is a minimal linear stochastic recurrent neural network model incorporating a dynamical gain term that depends on the total network activity. The dynamics are governed by coupled differential equations for neuron states and the gain parameter.
key_observables: Long-time autocorrelation function $C(t)$, which exhibits algebraic decay ($t^{-\alpha}$) when the spectrum is gapless, and the self-organized gain $a^*$.
important_parameters: The coupling strength $c$ (interaction strength), the noise variance $\sigma^2$, and the characteristic timescales $	au_x, 	au_a$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the recurrent matrix $M$ is symmetric (e.g., GOE) and that the gain unit only senses the total network activity ($\|x\|^2$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the emergence of an active fixed point at a critical coupling strength $c_{	ext{crit}}$. Figure 2 shows the deterministic flow spiraling into the active fixed point in the $(y_N, a)$ plane. Figure 3 confirms the $\propto t^{-1/2}$ power law decay of the normalized correlation function for various coupling strengths.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of fine-tuning in standard models. It then introduces the dynamical gain mechanism, deriving the coupled equations. The core analysis shows that the gain self-organizes to enforce criticality, leading to a stable critical phase characterized by power-law decay, independent of the initial coupling strength.
why_interesting: The mechanism of self-organization to maintain a critical state is a general principle applicable to many complex systems, including those studied in AMO physics where parameter tuning is often a major hurdle.
